To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) Change blindness is induced by brief interruptions that prevent visual representations from being stabilized.

(1) Change blindness occurs only when there are brief blank fields, and not when the blank fields are filled with random noise; (2) The duration of the blank fields is important, but not in a way that can be predicted from current models of the visual system; (3) Change blindness is not caused by an inability to remember the initial scene; (4) The duration of initial preview is important, but only when it is long; and (5) Change blindness occurs even when
the induced change blindness effect is dependent on initial preview and the nature of the interruption.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms of visual attention and the role of attention in the perception of change in complex visual scenes.
the question: What are the mechanisms that allow us to perceive the world around us?
understanding the nature of visual attention and how it is used to guide perception and behaviour.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the failure of change detection in scenes across brief interruptions is due to the inherent volatility of the representations at the early levels of visual processing and the need for focused attention to stabilize them.

“Change blindness is a consequence of the volatility of representations at the early stage of visual processing and the necessity of focused attention to stabilize them sufficiently for the perception of change”.
the change blindness phenomenon is a result of the failure of the observer to attend to the scene.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
change blindness is a failure of visual perception, not of memory.
change blindness is a consequence of the fact that visual representations are volatile.

change blindness can be induced by brief interruptions of the kind used in this study, and that the effects are not due to the failure to encode information in the original display or to the inability to maintain a stable internal representation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
change blindness is a failure of attention, and that it occurs when a change is presented in the context of a brief interruption.
change detection is not a unitary phenomenon.
we can induce “change blindness” by using brief blank interruptions between the displays.
